ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Neonatal cyanosis: 3

An infant who initially appeared well develops cyanosis and circulatory deterioration as the ductus arteriosus begins closing. The team requests urgent cardiology assessment. Which disease category must be considered because circulation may depend on continued ductal patency?

  1. Further clinical assessment and echocardiography when indicated
  2. Duct-dependent congenital heart disease
  3. Central cyanosis
  4. Peripheral acrocyanosis
  5. Compare right-hand and foot oxygen saturations
Answer and explanation

Duct-dependent congenital heart disease

Deterioration as the ductus closes can signal critical congenital heart disease requiring urgent specialist assessment and ductal support when indicated.

Option explanations

Duct-dependent congenital heart disease: Deterioration as the ductus closes can signal critical congenital heart disease requiring urgent specialist assessment and ductal support when indicated.

Central cyanosis: Blue discoloration of the tongue or oral mucosa suggests systemic arterial desaturation or an abnormal hemoglobin state and needs urgent evaluation. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Peripheral acrocyanosis: Bluish hands and feet with a pink tongue can reflect peripheral circulation rather than central hypoxemia; the overall clinical state still matters. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Compare right-hand and foot oxygen saturations: Right-hand measurement is preductal and a foot measurement is postductal; a difference can help assess ductal shunting but is not diagnostic by itself. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Further clinical assessment and echocardiography when indicated: A passed newborn oxygen screen does not exclude every important heart defect; new symptoms require assessment despite a previous pass. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
